paragraphs: A conversational agent can make sound decisions and still struggle when a user must carry them out. This paper introduces τ²-bench to evaluate that coordination problem. Existing benchmarks typically let only the agent change the environment, while users supply information. The new benchmark includes a telecommunications setting where both participants use tools to modify a shared world.

The environment represents a decentralized decision problem with partial observations. Tasks are assembled programmatically from smaller components, allowing the benchmark to vary complexity while keeping outcomes verifiable. Its user simulator is tied to the environment’s tools and observable state, so simulated user behavior is constrained by what is actually happening.

The evaluation also uses ablations to distinguish reasoning errors from communication and coordination errors. Experiments show substantial performance drops when agents move from acting without a user to sharing control with one. The result makes user guidance an explicit evaluation target: completing these tasks requires both choosing useful actions and communicating well enough for another participant to act successfully.
icml-2026-2-bench-evaluating-conversatio.tldr: τ²-bench tests conversational agents in a shared environment where success requires coordinating actions with an active user.

paragraphs: Diffusion models learn to generate data, but the order in which they learn different statistical relationships is less understood. This paper finds empirically that standard diffusion models trained on natural images learn pairwise relationships before more complicated correlations. That observation suggests a simplicity bias in how their knowledge develops during training.

To study the mechanism, the authors use simple denoisers and a controlled data model in which pairwise and higher-order correlations can be adjusted separately. They introduce a scalar quantity, the diffusion information exponent, that governs the sample complexity of learning these relationships. Within this setting, they prove linear sample complexity for pairwise statistics, while more complex statistics such as the fourth cumulant require at least cubic sample complexity.

The difficulty of higher-order learning changes when the statistics share structure. If pairwise and higher-order relationships have a correlated latent structure, the fourth cumulant can instead be learned with linear sample complexity. This conditional result explains how simpler relationships can support learning more complex ones, rather than complexity always imposing the same data requirement.
icml-2026-a-theory-of-learning-data-stat.tldr: A controlled theory explains why diffusion denoisers learn simpler statistics first and when shared latent structure makes complex statistics easier to learn.

paragraphs: Unrolling a recurrent neural network through time makes it resemble a deep network whose layers share weights. This paper asks how that structural difference produces different learned behavior. It develops a unified mean-field theory for fully trained recurrent and deep networks in the feature-learning regime, where training changes the representations themselves.

The theory describes representations through kernels and interprets training as Bayesian inference over sequences and patterns. For tasks typical of deep networks, it identifies a transition controlled by the strength of the learning signal relative to noise from random weights. Below the threshold, the two architectures behave identically within the theory. Above it, only recurrent networks develop correlated representations across time steps.

For sequential tasks, sharing weights also produces a bias that helps generalization by interpolating time steps that were not observed. These results connect an architectural choice to the organization of learned features. The contribution is a common theoretical account of when recurrent and deep networks behave alike, when their representations diverge, and how recurrence can support sequential generalization.
icml-2026-a-unified-theory-of-feature-le.tldr: A unified theory links recurrent weight sharing to a representation-learning phase transition and an inductive bias that aids sequential generalization.

paragraphs: Cyber defence agents trained with reinforcement learning often receive elaborate rewards that combine incentives and penalties for many states and actions. These signals help exploration, but they can also steer learning toward behavior that is suboptimal or risky. This paper examines how reward structure affects both training reliability and the defensive policies agents ultimately learn.

The evaluation compares sparse and dense rewards across two established cyber training environments, multiple network sizes, and both policy-gradient and value-based algorithms. A new ground-truth evaluation approach allows policies trained under different reward functions to be compared directly. That matters because each policy’s own training reward would otherwise provide a different yardstick for success.

The results favor sparse rewards when they align with defender goals and can be encountered frequently. Under those conditions, they produce more reliable training and more effective, lower-risk policies in the evaluation. Some policies also use costly defensive actions sparingly without explicit numerical penalties for those actions. The findings emphasize goal alignment and accessible feedback as key conditions for effective reward design.
icml-2026-beyond-rewards-in-rl-for-cyber.tldr: Goal-aligned sparse rewards that occur frequently improve training reliability and defensive behavior in the paper’s cyber defence evaluations.

paragraphs: Fast physical models often capture a system’s dominant behavior while leaving out interactions across smaller or faster scales. Cheap2Rich addresses the resulting gap between inexpensive simulation and complex physical systems. Its task is to reconstruct detailed system states from sparse sensor histories while retaining the computational advantages of a simpler model.

The framework combines a fast, low-fidelity prior with learned corrections for the discrepancy between that prior and higher-fidelity behavior. These corrections are designed to remain interpretable. The demonstration uses rotating detonation engines, where propagating detonation fronts interact with injector-driven fluctuations, mixing, and stiff chemistry across very different scales.

The reported results show successful reconstruction of high-fidelity engine states from sparse measurements. They also isolate physically meaningful discrepancy dynamics associated with injector effects, making the correction itself informative about the system. The paper presents this combination as a general approach to data assimilation and system identification, with potential value for rapid design exploration and real-time monitoring and control. Its central contribution is linking detailed reconstruction to an interpretable account of what the cheaper model misses.
icml-2026-cheap2rich-a-multi-fidelity-fr.tldr: Cheap2Rich combines fast physical models with interpretable learned corrections to reconstruct detailed rotating detonation engine states from sparse measurements.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. One intuitive approach trains a classifier to tell the collections apart. However, the reliability of conventional classifier-based tests hinges on a classifier being close to optimal, a demanding property that is difficult to verify.

This paper analyzes two conformal versions of that approach. They turn scores from any trained classifier, including weak, biased, or overfit classifiers, into exact finite-sample p-values. The authors establish control of false positives and nontrivial power, meaning an ability to detect genuine distributional differences. Power degrades gently as classifier error increases, separating reliable error control from the need for exceptionally accurate classification.

The framework is applied to checking neural posterior estimation models, which approximate Bayesian posterior distributions. Comparing an approximation with the true posterior becomes a two-sample testing problem. Across the reported benchmarks for this application, the conformal tests outperform classical discriminative tests. The findings make imperfect classifiers useful as statistical diagnostic tools while preserving an explicit account of their detection strength.
icml-2026-conformal-c2st-turning-weak-cl.tldr: Conformal calibration turns even weak classifier scores into valid two-sample tests whose detection power degrades gently with classifier error.

paragraphs: Users often give agents instructions with unstated intentions, missing parameters, mistaken assumptions, or ambiguous wording. For an agent that executes actions, misunderstanding those instructions can affect the environment. DRIFT-BENCH evaluates whether agents can repair such communication failures through multiple turns of clarification before or during grounded execution.

The benchmark organizes input faults using a taxonomy drawn from theories of cooperative communication. It covers both state-oriented and service-oriented execution environments, and combines a persona-driven user simulator with the Rise evaluation protocol. This setup makes clarification part of an ongoing interaction with a particular kind of user, rather than a single isolated response to an unclear prompt.

Experiments show substantial performance declines when these input faults are introduced. The usefulness of clarification also varies with the user persona and the type of fault. Those differences make the benchmark diagnostic: it can help reveal which communication breakdowns an agent handles poorly. The paper connects conversational clarification with agent evaluation by treating successful understanding as part of successful execution.
icml-2026-drift-bench-diagnosing-coopera.tldr: DRIFT-BENCH measures how agents clarify faulty user instructions across multiple turns and shows that such faults substantially reduce performance.

paragraphs: Layout-to-image generation uses object categories and spatial arrangements to control an image. When adapting to unusual domains from only a few examples, existing methods can produce fragmented or distorted results. This paper attributes that failure to representation fragmentation: object identity and visual details become entangled at incompatible levels of granularity.

The proposed framework separates stable semantic identity from reusable visual primitives. Semantic Anchoring aggregates category information into anchors that preserve what an object is. Primitive Imbuing models local visual building blocks that can be recombined. A third component, Conceptual Steering, uses a saliency-aware training objective to maintain semantic consistency in foreground objects.

Experiments in the five-example adaptation setting report consistent improvements over leading layout-to-image methods across diverse atypical domains. The gains concern both visual fidelity and alignment with the requested layout and content. Together, the components address how a model organizes its representation during adaptation: category identity remains stable while local detail can vary and recombine. The stated findings support this separation as a useful approach when examples are scarce and the target domain is unusual.
icml-2026-envisioning-beyond-the-few-dis.tldr: Separating object semantics from recomposable visual primitives improves five-shot layout-to-image adaptation across unusual domains.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a post-trained model can reveal the alignment data used to shape its capabilities and behavior. The authors report extracting significant amounts of such data, including material from supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Their focus includes training that supports long-context reasoning, safety, instruction following, and mathematics.

A central methodological point concerns how extraction is measured. Text matching can miss examples that retain the same meaning while differing in superficial form. The authors therefore use high-quality embedding models to assess semantic similarity. In their investigation, approximate string matching would conservatively have undercounted extractable data by a factor of ten because trivial artifacts depressed the matching score.

The extracted data also has practical training value: using it to train a base model recovers a meaningful amount of the original model’s performance. This finding connects data recovery with capability transfer. The authors identify a potentially overlooked exposure of alignment data and suggest that distillation may indirectly train on parts of a model’s original dataset when generated outputs reproduce that material.
icml-2026-extracting-alignment-data-in-o.tldr: Post-trained models can reveal useful alignment data, and semantic comparison detects substantially more extraction than string matching in this study.

paragraphs: Synthetic and auxiliary data can supplement limited real observations, but their value for statistical inference depends on how they are incorporated. This paper introduces General Synthetic-Powered Inference, or GESPI, as a wrapper around existing inference procedures. It combines real data with additional data generated by AI models or obtained from related tasks.

The framework adapts to the quality of the extra data. High-quality synthetic data increases statistical power, while poor-quality synthetic data causes the procedure to fall back to the standard method based on real data alone. The authors establish an error rate below a user-chosen bound without imposing distributional assumptions on the synthetic data, and report that error decreases as synthetic quality improves.

GESPI supports conformal prediction, risk control, hypothesis testing, and multiple testing without changing the underlying inference method. Demonstrations include protein structure prediction with AlphaFold and comparisons of reasoning models on difficult mathematics problems, both involving limited labeled data. The contribution is a general way to extract inferential value from additional data while maintaining explicit error control.
icml-2026-general-synthetic-powered-infe.tldr: GESPI uses useful synthetic data to strengthen statistical inference while preserving error control and falling back to real data when needed.

paragraphs: INDUCTION tests whether a model can discover a logical rule from examples in small relational worlds. Each problem supplies structures using a fixed vocabulary and labels objects that belong to an unknown concept. The model must produce one first-order formula that explains those labels across the supplied worlds.

The benchmark has three regimes. Full observation reveals every fact. Contrastive induction uses positive and negative worlds to demand hypotheses that discriminate between them. Existential completion allows unknown facts, with validity determined by whether each world admits a suitable completion. Because the domains are finite, proposed formulas can be checked exactly through evaluation and satisfiability-modulo-theories methods.

The study evaluates frontier language models alongside symbolic synthesis baselines, measuring both correctness and formula size. Prompted models show meaningful but incomplete capability, with pronounced difficulty differences and challenging structural families. On held-out examples, compact formulas generalize much better than bloated ones. This result makes parsimony informative: a short rule is more likely in these evaluations to capture the underlying concept rather than merely fit the observed finite worlds.
icml-2026-induction-finite-structure-con.tldr: INDUCTION evaluates logical rule discovery in finite worlds and finds that compact formulas generalize substantially better than bloated ones.

paragraphs: A junta distribution has probabilities that depend on only a small subset of its input bits. This paper studies how efficiently such distributions, their quantum counterparts, and related quantum circuits can be learned. For a distribution depending on k of n bits, it proves a sample bound proportional to 2^k log(n)/ε² for total-variation error ε, matching the existing lower bound in every parameter.

The quantum analogue consists of an arbitrary k-qubit state together with maximally mixed remaining qubits. The authors establish learning bounds of O(12^k log(n)/ε²) copies and complementary lower bounds. Testing whether an unknown state is close to this family is much more demanding: for constant k, distinguishing ε-closeness from 7ε-farness requires exponentially many copies in n, up to logarithmic factors.

The paper also shows that QAC⁰ circuits are close to juntas and improves their learning bounds using copies of a circuit’s Choi state. Additional results give a Pauli-analysis proof of optimal Classical Shadows performance and stronger circuit lower bounds for the address function. Together, the results clarify both the benefits and limits of exploiting dependence on few variables.
icml-2026-learning-junta-distributions-q.tldr: The paper establishes optimal classical junta learning rates, quantum junta learning and testing bounds, and improved learning bounds for QAC⁰ circuits.

paragraphs: An agent’s observations can contain far more information than it needs to control its environment. This paper asks whether learning through action can produce representations that retain control-relevant information while ignoring irrelevant variation. It studies empowerment, an objective that encourages an agent to maximize its influence over the environment and is used for unsupervised skill learning.

The analysis shows that empowerment agents induce two representations, described as forward and backward. These capture complementary aspects of the state, and both are invariant to features that do not matter for control. Such invariance means those irrelevant features do not change the representation. Together, the representations form an implicit model of the world organized around the agent’s ability to affect it.

The result gives interaction a central role in representation learning. In the authors’ analysis, interaction directed toward maximizing control is essential to obtaining the useful invariances, connecting the work to causal learning. The contribution is an account of how a control objective can shape perception itself, selecting information according to its relevance for action.
icml-2026-learning-to-perceive-the-world.tldr: Empowerment induces complementary representations that ignore control-irrelevant features and organize the world around an agent’s influence.

paragraphs: Matroid algorithms often rely on an independence oracle that decides whether a chosen set satisfies the matroid’s independence rules. Standard analysis charges the same amount for every query, regardless of set size. This paper replaces that abstraction with a cost proportional to the queried set’s size, reflecting the work needed by natural implementations more faithfully.

Under this model, the authors study finding a basis, approximating rank, and approximating partition size. They give explicit algorithms and nearly matching lower bounds, showing that optimal query cost is quadratic in the matroid size up to logarithmic factors. The lower bounds are unconditional and apply even to weaker versions that only distinguish between possibilities, strengthening the computational barrier.

The paper also identifies a structural condition that allows faster algorithms. When every circuit has size at most c, a maximum-weight basis can be computed with expected query cost O(n^(2−1/c) log n). Thus, accounting for query size changes the general complexity picture while still exposing useful advantages for restricted matroid families.
icml-2026-matroid-algorithms-under-size-.tldr: Charging matroid queries by set size yields near-quadratic complexity barriers, with faster maximum-weight basis algorithms when circuit size is bounded.

paragraphs: Demonstrations, comparisons, ratings, rankings, and stop signals each express preferences differently. Reward-learning systems commonly use one feedback type or combine several through manually weighted losses. MAVRL instead treats them as evidence about a shared, unknown reward function, allowing each form of feedback to contribute through its own probabilistic likelihood.

The method uses amortized variational inference to learn a distribution over rewards efficiently. A shared encoder represents the reward, while feedback-specific likelihood decoders connect it to the different observed signals. Training optimizes one evidence lower bound. This formulation avoids converting all feedback into a common intermediate format and removes the need to manually balance separate loss terms.

Across discrete and continuous-control benchmarks, jointly inferred reward distributions outperform single-feedback baselines and exploit complementary information from the different feedback types. Policies learned from them are also more robust to environment perturbations in the reported experiments. Because the output includes uncertainty about reward, the method provides interpretable signals for examining confidence and consistency across feedback sources, alongside the reward estimate used for control.
icml-2026-mavrl-learning-reward-function.tldr: MAVRL combines heterogeneous feedback through Bayesian reward inference, improving learned policies while exposing uncertainty and cross-feedback consistency.

paragraphs: Most graph neural networks update vertices by exchanging messages with neighboring vertices. This paper develops an alternative centered on edges and triangles. It introduces an edge-based graph refinement test, EB-1WL, and a corresponding neural architecture, EB-GNN, inspired by a classic triangle-counting algorithm.

The theoretical analysis shows that EB-1WL can distinguish substantially more graph structure than the standard 1WL test. The authors characterize its capabilities using first-order logic and results based on counting graph homomorphisms. These tools describe which structural differences the method can recognize, giving a formal account of its expressive power beyond architectural intuition.

Greater expressivity often increases computational demands, so the paper also analyzes efficiency. It proves near-linear time and memory usage for EB-1WL and EB-GNN on practical graph-learning workloads. Experiments show that EB-GNN substantially outperforms simple message-passing networks and remains competitive with specialized leading architectures at substantially lower computational cost. The findings support edge-and-triangle message passing as a general-purpose way to combine richer structural reasoning with practical scalability.
icml-2026-message-passing-on-the-edge-to.tldr: EB-GNN passes messages through edges and triangles to gain stronger graph expressivity while retaining near-linear costs on practical workloads.

paragraphs: A visual patch representation can mix several distinct elements, making it hard for a multimodal language model to focus on the detail requested by an instruction. MoDA addresses this entanglement with a lightweight adapter that changes how individual feature channels contribute. The instruction determines which embedding dimensions receive emphasis.

The adapter applies cross-attention between language instructions and already-aligned visual features to produce dynamic modulation masks. Those masks act multiplicatively at the channel level, differing from token-level additive feature selection. The method follows the standard LLaVA training protocol and requires no additional supervision or architectural modifications.

The evaluation spans twelve benchmarks covering visual question answering, visual reasoning, and hallucination detection across three model families. Reported gains include twelve points on MMVP for LLaVA-1.5 and improvements on ScienceQA, RealWorldQA, and GQA in other families. The additional computation is below one percent of FLOPs. Consistent gains across the evaluated families, including beyond CLIP-based encoders, support instruction-guided channel modulation as an efficient way to improve fine-grained visual grounding.
icml-2026-moda-modulation-adapter-for-fi.tldr: MoDA uses instruction-guided channel modulation to improve fine-grained visual understanding across three multimodal model families with minimal computational overhead.

paragraphs: This paper studies binary classification when information is distributed across a network of agents. Each agent sees only some feature coordinates and receives prediction logits from its predecessors in a directed acyclic graph. It fits a logistic predictor using its local features and incoming logits, then forwards its own logit downstream.

The main question is whether this sequence can approach the best logistic predictor that sees every feature directly. The authors prove an excess-loss upper bound of O(M/√D) along paths of depth D satisfying a coverage condition: every consecutive block of M agents must collectively observe all features. This makes both repeated feature coverage and network depth explicit parts of the guarantee.

The paper also constructs difficult instances with excess loss at least Ω(k/D), where k is the number of features. The upper and lower bounds together identify depth as a fundamental constraint on information aggregation. Extending such analysis from squared-loss regression to logistic classification requires handling binary cross-entropy directly, providing a theoretical account of when sequential prediction sharing can combine distributed information.
icml-2026-networked-information-aggregat.tldr: Sequential logit sharing can aggregate distributed classification features under a coverage condition, with network depth constraining achievable excess loss.

paragraphs: Neural scaling laws describe how model performance improves as resources increase. One proposed explanation is that they inherit power laws already present in the data. This paper examines that idea using transformers trained to predict random walks on graphs whose complexity can be controlled, finding scaling laws even without power laws in the data correlations.

The authors also simplify language progressively by generating training sequences with language models of decreasing depth, down to bigram models. The resulting scaling exponents evolve monotonically as this complexity changes. Experiments with random walks include both Erdős–Rényi graphs and scale-free Barabási–Albert graphs, providing additional controlled settings for studying the phenomenon.

Returning to language modeling, the paper reproduces several essential scaling results using two-layer transformers with a context length of one hundred. It also presents an alternative way to obtain compute-optimal curves. Preliminary evidence suggests maximal update parameterization may use parameters more efficiently than standard parameterization. Overall, the findings show that comparatively simple settings can expose scaling behavior and help investigate its origins.
icml-2026-on-the-origin-of-neural-scalin.tldr: Controlled graph and language experiments show that neural scaling laws can emerge without power-law data correlations and change with task complexity.

paragraphs: Observing players’ actions does not directly reveal the incentives behind them. This paper studies a learner who sees two players’ actions while they play an exact or approximate Nash equilibrium of a bimatrix game. The learner knows neither the underlying game nor the equilibrium and seeks payoffs that could explain the observed behavior.

The target is the entire set of compatible payoffs. This set-valued formulation retains the range of incentive structures consistent with the evidence. The authors measure estimation accuracy using Hausdorff distance, which compares sets through how closely their points can be matched, and seek guarantees that hold with high probability at a chosen precision.

The paper establishes the first minimax-optimal rates for this problem, covering exact and approximate equilibrium play in both zero-sum and general-sum games. Minimax optimality characterizes the best achievable worst-case estimation rate. These results give learning-theoretic foundations for inferring incentives from behavior, supporting downstream uses such as counterfactual analysis and mechanism design that need to account for multiple plausible payoff functions.
icml-2026-optimal-rates-for-feasible-pay.tldr: The paper establishes minimax-optimal rates for estimating all payoff functions consistent with observed exact or approximate equilibrium behavior.

paragraphs: A deployed policy can change the environment in which it operates, shifting the dynamics that determine its future outcomes. Performative reinforcement learning studies this feedback between decisions and environment change. This paper develops policy-gradient methods that account explicitly for those policy-induced shifts.

The authors prove performative versions of two foundational reinforcement-learning results: the performance difference lemma and the policy gradient theorem. These results support Performative Policy Gradient, or PePG. Under softmax parameterization, they prove convergence to performatively optimal policies both with and without entropy regularization. The guarantee concerns policies evaluated with the distribution shifts their own deployment induces.

This advances beyond prior methods aimed at performative stability, a target that does not itself establish optimality. Empirical evaluations on standard performative reinforcement-learning environments also show PePG outperforming existing stability-oriented algorithms. The contribution combines a revised mathematical basis for comparing and improving policies with an algorithm that targets optimal behavior in environments affected by the learner itself, rather than treating those induced changes as outside the learning problem.
icml-2026-performative-policy-gradient-o.tldr: PePG accounts for policy-induced environment shifts and has convergence guarantees to performatively optimal policies under softmax parameterization.

paragraphs: Steering vectors offer a lightweight way to influence a language model’s behavior, but their strength must often be tuned carefully to preserve generation quality. Intervening throughout the generated sequence can also damage quality even with careful tuning. This paper addresses both the training of steering strength and where intervention occurs.

First, the authors jointly train each steering vector’s direction and strength, removing the need to select the strength afterward. Their scaling-theory analysis finds that moderately large initial values and learning rates for steering factors are essential to stable, efficient joint training. Second, they introduce Prompt-Only Steering Vector, or PrOSV, which modifies only a few prompt tokens.

With the joint training scheme, PrOSV outperforms traditional full-sequence steering vectors on AxBench. It also achieves a better empirical tradeoff between general utility and adversarial robustness. These findings support concentrating intervention in the prompt while learning its strength together with its direction. The reported benefit is an improved tradeoff, rather than a claim that steering eliminates every cost to model quality.
icml-2026-towards-steering-without-sacri.tldr: Jointly training steering direction and strength while intervening only on prompt tokens improves the measured steering and utility tradeoffs.

paragraphs: A foundation model’s final layer is not necessarily where all useful information for a new task resides. This paper finds that task-relevant information varies non-monotonically across depth and cannot be recovered through naive aggregation. Its geometric and empirical analysis examines both which layers distinguish task categories and how their embeddings are organized.

The proposed Layer-wise Optimal Embedding Selection method, LOES, uses spectral analysis to identify task-discriminative subspaces. It minimizes residual error subject to orthogonality and isotropy constraints, making the geometry of the selected representation part of the objective. The authors also introduce Geometric Regularization, which encourages a simplicial arrangement of class manifolds and stabilizes representation geometry during fine-tuning.

Across the evaluated architectures, modalities, depths, and data regimes, LOES consistently outperforms standard baselines, with larger gains as model depth increases. The method also reveals how semantic factors are distributed across layers, supporting cross-lingual and cross-modal interpretability analyses. The results indicate that effective transfer depends on selecting and organizing intermediate information, giving layer geometry a substantive role in how pretrained knowledge is reused.
icml-2026-uncovering-the-latent-potentia.tldr: LOES selects geometrically organized, task-relevant subspaces across model layers and improves transfer across the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models use extensive pretraining to forecast unseen sequences without task-specific fine-tuning. This paper examines what their internal components contribute. Across evaluations of leading transformer-based models, it finds redundant intermediate components and reports that every model studied remains robust when entire layers are ablated.

The authors introduce interpretability tools that remove selected components and trace their direct contributions through the residual stream. They apply these tools across diverse architectures and real-world and synthetic datasets. A theoretical view of transformers as kernel regressors further motivates selecting attention heads for ablation using the stable rank of their projection matrices, an intrinsic property of the model.

This head-selection approach identifies particular heads responsible for undesirable patterns, including repetition of motifs from the context and a bias toward seasonality. The results connect internal structure with recognizable forecasting behavior. Their consistency across the studied models suggests shared properties within this emerging model class, while the component-level analysis offers a way to investigate both redundant computation and the mechanisms behind specific prediction tendencies.
icml-2026-universal-redundancies-in-time.tldr: The studied time-series foundation models tolerate whole-layer ablations, while specific attention heads drive motif repetition and seasonality bias.

paragraphs: VocSim evaluates whether frozen audio embeddings place acoustically different instances of the same content near one another. It aggregates 125,000 single-source clips from nineteen corpora spanning speech, animal vocalizations, and environmental sounds. Polyphonic mixtures are outside its scope, keeping the focus on content representation without the additional problem of separating sound sources.

The benchmark updates no model parameters and uses label-free PCA whitening within each subset to correct embedding anisotropy. It measures local retrieval purity with Precision@k and point-wise class separation with Global Separation Rate, calibrated against an empirical permutation baseline. A simple pipeline combining frozen Whisper features, time–frequency pooling, and PCA achieves strong zero-shot results.

The findings also expose a specific generalization gap: on blind evaluations of low-resource Shipibo-Conibo and Chintang speech, local retrieval deteriorates sharply while staying above chance. External validation shows that the strongest embeddings predict avian perceptual similarity, improve bioacoustic classification, and achieve state-of-the-art HEAR performance. The benchmark therefore reveals both useful transferable structure and weaknesses that ordinary adaptation-based evaluations can leave unexplored.
icml-2026-vocsim-a-training-free-benchma.tldr: VocSim tests frozen audio embeddings without model training, finding strong cross-domain content structure alongside a low-resource speech retrieval gap.
